#2024. Ukraine vs Georgia - prediction, team news, lineups

By Ellis Stevens | 15 Nov 2026 16:54

Ukraine welcome Georgia to Kosicka futbalova arena on Tuesday night for a matchday six clash in UEFA Nations League B Group 2.

The hosts are third in the standings and two points ahead of their bottom-placed visitors, leaving both teams fighting to confirm their survival in League B.

Ukraine got their 2026-27 Nations League campaign underway with an encouraging 1-0 victory over Hungary, with Danylo Sikan scoring the only goal just before half-time.

After following that result up with a 0-0 draw against Georgia, Ukraine have subsequently fallen to three consecutive defeats, losing 3-0 and 1-0 to Northern Ireland and 2-1 to Hungary.

Andrea Maldera's side, as a result, sit third in Nations League B Group 2 with four points from five matches, and with just one game remaining, Ukraine are unable to climb into the promotion playoff places.

However, Ukraine are still fighting to ensure their survival in League B, as they lead visitors Georgia by only two points, meaning defeat on Tuesday would consign Maldera's men to a relegation playoff fixture.

Ukraine will secure their League B status with at least a draw, and they will, therefore, be hoping to replicate or improve upon their 0-0 stalemate with Georgia in the reverse fixture.

Georgia have failed to win any of their five League B matches, recording two draws and suffering three defeats during that time.

Despite boasting the likes of Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and Georges Mikautadze in attack, Georgia have also failed to find the back of the net in any of their five matches, while they have conceded four times.

Georgia will be hoping to end their goalless streak when they come up against Ukraine, who have conceded more than any other team in the group (six conceded).

However, Georgia's attack has been weakened by the long-term injury to Kvaratskhelia, who scored the nation's last goal in their 2-0 victory over Bahrain in a friendly in June.

Georgia will also have to overcome a miserable record in meetings with Ukraine, having failed to defeat Tuesday's opponents in any of their 12 meetings - losing seven and drawing five.

Ukraine failed to find the net for the third time in Group 2 as they lost 1-0 to Northern Ireland last time out, and Maldera may opt to make changes in attack as a result, meaning the likes of Artem Dovbyk could start.

At the opposite end, captain Mykola Matvienko could start alongside Ilya Zabarnyi, with Illia Krupskyi introduced at right-back.

Meanwhile, Georgia will be without superstar Kvaratskhelia due to a long-term injury, meaning much of the attacking responsibility will rest on Mikautadze's shoulders.

The striker should be supported by Zuriko Davitashvili, Nika Gagnidze and Giorgi Kvernadze, with Anzor Mekvabishvili and Giorgi Chakvetadze in midfield.

#2023. Gila explains how he went from ‘rock bottom’ at Lazio to joining Milan: “More kindness”

Mario Gila has explained how he managed to get through a difficult time at the start of his Italy adventure, eventually performing at such a high level that AC Milan decided to sign him.

Gila left Real Madrid and Spain in the summer of 2022, when he was just 21 years old, as Lazio secured his services. In his first season, however, he only got 765 minutes on the pitch and didn’t play a single game in the second half of the campaign.

The following season, it was as if things had changed completely, as the centre-back started performing really well and was rewarded with a lot of playing time. The growth only continued from there, resulting in Milan paying good money for him in the summer.

In his long interview with AC Milan for the interview series The Chamber, Gila discussed his initial struggles in Italy, hitting ‘rock bottom’ in his first season with Lazio. A psychologist and a changed mindset helped him get through it all.

When you make a mistake, are you very demanding and hard on yourself? I mean, how do you treat yourself when something doesn’t go the way you wanted?

“In the past, for example… I’ve changed a great deal. I went through a really difficult time early in my career here in Italy and hit rock bottom, but with outside help, psychological support, I got through it.

“That’s why I keep saying ‘before’. Back then, I was very hard on myself. I didn’t allow myself to fail. If I did, I was extremely negative towards myself, I couldn’t accept that I might fail or make mistakes.

“Now I handle it much better. Now I feel that making mistakes is part of the job, it’s something that helps you improve, something that helps you grow. So I deal with it much more calmly, I process it much better internally.

“I think you still need to hold yourself to high standards and you also need to know how to find a solution to that mistake, whether in your career or in your personal life, but with much more calm and more kindness towards myself.”

Regarding that difficult period you went through, which helped you grow and taught you so many things, you mentioned therapy. Could you tell me, not so much what happened, but what your experience with therapy was like? I mean, what did it give you at first?

“I sought help from a psychologist because I was going through a very difficult time and couldn’t find a way to move forward. We’re expected to deal with situations… that I find mentally overwhelming, at just 21 years old, when you have no professional experience, because in the end, everything comes at you so fast.

“So I went to a psychologist, and completely changed my perspective. I mean, I started seeing everything negative that happened to me as a step forward, thinking: this is something that will help you improve, something you needed to go through.

“Everything changed when I changed my perspective. I used to be very hard on myself, very hard, I demanded so much of myself. Now I’m someone who feels much more at ease.

“We can all fail, make mistakes, go through difficult situations, So the way I treat myself, the way I respond to myself, the way I talk to myself, I think it plays a crucial role in maintaining a consistently positive mindset.”

#2022. ‘I felt my leg…’ – Dominik Szoboszlai makes worrying injury admission after Hungary win

Dominik Szoboszlai has given an update on his knee injury after Hungary’s win over Georgia on Saturday, and his comments could be quite concerning for Liverpool fans.

The midfielder’s involvement for his country during this international window was placed in doubt after the knock that he incurred in the Reds’ victory at Crystal Palace last weekend, although he still linked up with Marco Rossi’s squad for their UEFA Nations League fixtures.

The Hungarian FA had deferred any decision on whether the 26-year-old would play until the last minute, but he featured for the entirety of his nation’s 2-0 triumph in Tbilisi and claimed the assist for Barnabas Varga’s clinching goal.

Szoboszlai revealed after the match that he nearly pulled out of playing after he felt a twinge during the warm-up prior to kick-off, but his determination to feature would eventually prevail.

In quotes relayed by Nemzeti Sport, the Hungary captain said: “I was always 100% sure that I would be able to play, but the doctors were less sure. I progressed day by day, focused on myself, received treatment.

“I played with my leg for a training session and a half, and in the warm-up I was close to cancelling it because I felt my leg on one of the shots, but if I’ve come this far, I won’t let the team down. Now the treatment starts all over again. I have to be ready again by Tuesday.”

Szoboszlai’s comments may well come as a worry to Liverpool fans, with the midfielder admitting that he played through the pain barrier and seemingly defied the assessment of medical professionals.

His remark about getting ready for Hungary’s match against Northern Ireland on Tuesday night will also have Andoni Iraola sweating, with the 26-year-old set to push himself for a tight turnaround even though he seems nowhere near full fitness.

It’s natural that, as captain of his country, the Reds’ number 8 will stop at nothing to try and be available for them, but his club will be left praying that he comes through the Magyars’ next game unscathed.

Szoboszlai will return from international duty into a hectic run of 11 Liverpool fixtures before the end of December, and we’ll need him and his teammates to be operating at their best throughout that busy period.

For everyone at Anfield, Hungary’s match on Tuesday will be monitored with frayed nerves to see if the midfielder comes through without any further complications in his knee.

#2021. Rafa Benitez now looking at job with Premier League club

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Rafa Benitez has been talking about making a return to the Premier League.

The Spanish manager having previously been in charge at Liverpool, Chelsea, Newcastle United and Everton.

Rafa Benitez revealing that he has turned down a number of national team jobs in recent months, as well as clubs in both Mexico and Brazil.

The one-time Real Madrid boss telling The Athletic that now his priority is a Premier League job next.

Now 66, Rafa Benitez was sacked by Everton in 2022 and since then has only managed Celta Vigo and Panathinaikos.

The former Newcastle United manager lasting only nine months in Spain and eight months in Greece before getting the sack both times.

Rafa Benitez explaining to The Athletic: “For me, the priority is the Premier League. After you go Italy, Spain, Germany and France. In general, the Premier League has the most money and is able to buy the best players. You have some fantastic teams in Spain and Italy, but I like the atmosphere in the Premier League. I’m not just watching games; I’m analysing with a tactical vision, trying to learn something new which I could implement. I don’t just want to be in a job; I want to be sure I can compete for something — whether that’s staying in the division, qualifying for Europe or winning something. I want to stay in Europe. Maybe I’ll have to go to China but that’s not the idea. There will come a point where if you cannot get what you want, you have to make a decision.”

Rafa Benitez on how his future club would ideally look: “It has to be somewhere they respect your vision and experience…Are you creating something for the future? Is everyone on the same page? You need a clear vision and communication across the club, and time to improve a team. When you have had success in different countries, when you’ve had to handle difficult situations, when you know the mentality of players, you can manage in a different way and get the best out of them. Young people, especially, don’t attach too much value to experience, but after all these years, I’m a better coach than I’ve ever been.”

During the interview, Rafa Benitez talked about his previous Premier League jobs and said about his time at Newcastle United under Mike Ashley: “We achieved something very difficult. We made a £30m profit (on player transfers) and won the Championship. Then we finished 10th and 13th in the Premier League without spending big money. That was a great achievement.”

#2020. England lineup vs. Spain confirmed as Ben White starts in triple change

By Ben Knapton | 15 Nov 2026 18:34, Last updated: 15 Nov 2026 18:46

England and Spain have confirmed their starting lineups for Sunday's UEFA Nations League showdown at the Metropolitano Stadium.

Thomas Tuchel's men must beat the world and European champions to win League A Group 3, although both sides have already sealed their spots in the quarter-finals.

The Three Lions have made three changes for their reunion with La Roja, all of which come in defence, including the already-known switch in goal between James Trafford and Jordan Pickford.

Tuchel has also brought Ben White - who was once again booed by England fans against Croatia on Thursday - back into the starting XI, at the expense of Trent Alexander-Arnold.

Fellow Arsenal man Ezri Konsa is also restored to the starting lineup after missing the midweek victory through injury, taking Dan Burn's place in the heart of defence.

Djed Spence and Myles Lewis-Skelly must make do with spots on the bench following their returns from injury and suspension respectively, as Tuchel sticks with an unchanged midfield and attacking selection.

As for Spain, head coach Luis de la Fuente has made five changes to the side that bested the Czech Republic 2-0 last time out, including expected recalls for Lamine Yamal and Mikel Oyarzabal.

The pair both missed Spain's penultimate group game as a precautionary measure, but they have unsurprisingly been selected over Yeremy Pino and Ferran Torres this time around.

De la Fuente has also made a bold call in the number 10 role, demoting Fermin Lopez in favour of Mikel Merino, but Alex Baena hold his spot on the left over Nico Williams - now fully fit again following illness.

Merino's Arsenal teammate Martin Zubimendi is also retained in midfield over Pedri, despite concerns over fatigue having played the full 90 against the Czech Republic amid a lack of game time at club level.

De la Fuente has made two changes to his backline foe the final matchday, as Marc Pubill replaces Pedro Porro at right-back, and Aymeric Laporte is in for Dean Huijsen in central defence.

England XI: Trafford; White, Konsa, Quansah, Hall; Anderson, Rice; Rogers, Ju. Bellingham, Gordon; Kane

Subs: Pickford, Alexander-Arnold, Steele, Gibbs-White, Spence, Burn, Jo. Bellingham, Hill, Calvert-Lewin, Ngumoha, Eze, Lewis-Skelly

Spain XI: Simon; Pubill, Cubarsi, Laporte, Cucurella; Zubimendi, Ruiz; Yamal, Merino, Baena; Oyarzabal

Subs: Raya, Garcia, Roca, Huijsen, Torres. Lopez, Pino, Porro, Barrios, Munoz, Williams, Pedri

There’ll be some relief amongst the West Ham medical staff at Rush Green tonight knowing that Manor Solomon was left out of Israel’s match altogether after the winger could not train owing to the pain of an ongoing injury.

However there will be concern that this same issue which dogged Solomon through September might yet prevent him playing his full part in the busy run up to Christmas  – with its demanding schedule of nine games in a little over a month.

Solomon – early season form has fallen away as his back injury has made itself known

#2018. Why Newcastle United the football club is an entity which I find increasingly loathsome

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Over nearly forty years of supporting Newcastle United, there are few things more certain than the knowledge that this club will let me down time and again.

In terms of what happens on the field, that is part and parcel of being a football supporter. After all, there are 92 league clubs and it stands to reason that the vast majority of those teams will only watch on, frustrated, while a small minority achieve success.

To that end, on the law of averages we are very fortunate to support a club that has spent its entire existence in the top two tiers of English football, most of my lifetime in the top division and even won a trophy a couple of years back.

So in that context, you can be pragmatic about the failures, enjoy the successes when they come and proudly tell the players in black and white that “we’ll support you ever more”.

Yet it is the club’s activity off the field that really gets my goat. I hate to say it, but while the club has stabilised since the takeover, improved as a commercial entity and enjoyed a bit of silverware for the first time in forever, it has also lost its soul.

“Our fans are the beating heart of Newcastle United,” declared CEO David Hopkinson as he announced the latest season ticket price hike earlier this year.

In 2025, he told the Newcastle United Supporters Trust: “Supporters are at the heart of everything we do.” Meanwhile, chairman Yasir Al-Rumayyan claimed our support “will never be taken for granted” in an open letter to fans back in 2022.

We are absolutely taken for granted. And if we are at the heart of what the club does, it is in the most transactional sense possible – as paying lemmings who are a guaranteed source of income.

Take my experience of trying to get tickets for my sons for the Sunderland game as a prime example.

To be clear, I fully understand that match tickets are at a premium and for this game more than any other, demand would have been huge.

Imagine my surprise, then, when my two sons were seemingly successful in the ballot.

Given the club claim it is a strike rate of one in seven yet this was my eldest son’s first successful ballot in 22 attempts and my youngest son’s first in 15, this was a particularly welcome stroke of luck.

Worse still, because we tried to have him accompany my elder son in the family area, neither were allowed to utilise their ballot success, as my eldest was automatically disqualified when he no longer had a youth to accompany him.

Now I totally understand why these rules exist. Our situation was an unfortunate quirk of when my youngest son’s birthday fell and was an error made in good faith, but it would be very easy for people to exploit this and fill the family section with adults if the club were not vigilant. I get that and I respect that.

That is why I accept when I phoned the Box Office to try to resolve this unforeseen anomaly they were unable to provide us with tickets in that area.

What was less easy to accept was the absolute wall of intransigence and unhelpfulness I was faced with.

Could we get tickets in a different area? “No, you’ve won the ballot in that area so that’s it”.

Why does the website block us from buying the tickets now but did not block us from entering a ballot that it turns out we could never win? “It is your responsibility to enter the ballot in the right area.”

Can we not just have two tickets elsewhere given that the allocation that goes on general sale will be unchanged – we will not be using the two we have won so it will be the same net figure? “No, the policy does not allow that. It would not be fair on other supporters.”

The ballot system is inherently unfair as our strike rate shows – we have had a rare success and now we cannot use it because the system allowed us to enter a ballot we could not win. Is that fair? “I’m not prepared to depart from the policy.”

As anyone who has encountered our Supporter Services will know, escalating the matter to them was about as effective as the experiment of playing Nick Woltemade as a number 8.

Some will say I should not base my view of the club on interactions with a handful of lower paid staff working in the Box Office and Supporter Services. I disagree.

Senior leaders in any organisation set the culture. If David Hopkinson truly believed supporters are the “beating heart” of Newcastle United, he and his executive team would have led the behaviours that set the tone for everyone else.

Interactions with the frontline staff are the very best test for what an organisation really values, and I can tell you now that Newcastle United does not value its supporters beyond the transactional purpose they serve.

Allow me to give another example. Last season, my sister won two tickets in the ballot to take her son to see Newcastle play Bournemouth.

Now my sister is a proper fan. Growing up in Hexham, she spent most of her teen years trying to hang around Causey Hill in Hexham long enough to wave at the passing cars of Mick Quinn, Ray Ranson, Kevin Brock and Mark McGhee, who lived at the top of the road. She even became Roy Aitken’s family babysitter!

She started going to games during the desperate 1988-89 season which ended in relegation and has been a regular at home and away games ever since.

Now living in the south east, getting to home games is an effort and the Bournemouth game last season proved to be a particular trial.

Train delay after train delay resulted in that trip becoming akin to the Griswalds’ trip to Wally World in National Lampoon’s Vacation: rather than it being a day out, it became a mission.

After the first delay they knew it would be tight for kick-off, by the second they knew they would miss some of the first half, by the next they were hoping to get in for the second half, and by the time they eventually arrived it was a case of: “We’ve come this far, we might as well watch the last 10 minutes!”

Off they bombed sprinting up Pink Lane to get to the ground, only to arrive in around the 80th minute and be turned away by the stewards. They presented their tickets, they told them what they had been through, but it was all to no avail. Supporter Services on the day were actually very supportive; those based at the ground said the stewards had made the wrong call and if they called up on Monday they would “see what they could do.”

It turned out, what they could do was never tested: what they would do was absolutely nothing. Supporter Services denied any knowledge of the response they had been given on the Saturday, and virtually accused my sister of making the whole thing up.

“Supporters are at the heart of everything we do”, are they Mr Hopkinson? Well that is not the experience most of us face when interacting with the people you field to manage those relationships.

No, this is a club which has lost its heart.

You need look no further than the utterly dreadful rendition of Blaydon Races which they have forced us to endure on matchdays to understand quite how much the decision-makers at Newcastle United do not understand what our club is. What used to set us apart in home games was the intensity and atmosphere that the crowd brought. Messrs Keegan, Robson and Howe all understood that.

When I was at the depressing Everton game recently, I could not help but think immediately before kick-off ahead of both the first and second halves how the people who make those decisions are strangling the life out of what we are.

If ever there was a way to sap the atmosphere out of the crowd when you need them most it would be by drowning them out with a funeral-march rendition of the Geordie anthem being played at full blast through the stadium speakers. It even killed the Strawberry Corner.

You look at other things – like that dreadful variation on our club badge – and wonder what on earth motivates these people to make the decisions that they do.

The new version looks like some awful re-hash of the original created for a computer game to avoid copyright infringement.

I mean, seriously, was it worth the upset and cost of changing a crest we have known and loved for decades just to introduce that abomination?

I will always love Newcastle United, because it is part of me. That is why, despite Yasir Al-Rummayan’s protestations to the contrary, it is so easy for the powers that be to take us for granted, which they do unreservedly and indiscriminately. We are hooked in by the nostalgia, the memories, the stories, the glorious moments.

Maybe we are motivated by that truly united feeling of togetherness when you are packed into the concourse at any away ground, chanting for 20 minutes non-stop just for each other and the looks on the faces of the bemused home stewards because there’s not a player or opposition supporter in sight.

Perhaps we are driven by the hope, or the sheer unbridled joy of that last-minute winner or a hard-fought victory against one of the league’s elite.

Or for some of us it is just a way of life. Something we did with our mum or dad and now we do with our children, and one day when they are mums and dads they will do with their children too.

In more crass terms, a cynic might say we are victims of Stockholm Syndrome: a condition in which people develop an emotional attachment, affection or loyalty to their captor or abuser.

However much we love Newcastle United, we should never be allow ourselves to forget that it is a love which is utterly unrequited. We are commodities to buy tickets, buy shirts and create an image of fervour that can be sold as a commercial package to the highest bidder.

The members’ general sale tickets for Sunderland sold out within minutes. Yet there is still plenty of room if you are prepared to pay £800 for your ticket, along with  bit of food and the brief musings of one of Keegan’s Entertainers pre and post-match.

While Newcastle United the football team remains something I seem bound to unconditionally love despite all my senses telling me I should not, Newcastle United the football club is an entity which I find increasingly loathsome.

#2017. USA vs Haiti - prediction, team news, lineups

By Joel Lefevre | 15 Nov 2026 19:06

On Tuesday, the USA aim to give their manager a fitting send-off when they host Haiti in the second leg of that quarter-final CONCACAF Nations League tie at TQL Stadium in Cincinnati.

It would require an epic collapse for the Yanks to be eliminated from this tournament on Tuesday, having beaten the Haitians 6-0 in leg one.

For the final time, Mauricio Pochettino will be on the US sidelines Tuesday, hoping to end his tenure on a positive note before heading to Old Trafford to join Manchester United.

While he leaves the national team program without a trophy, the Argentine coach has seen this team flourish since the World Cup concluded, and they are currently on a five-match winning run across all competitions.

Pochettino’s men have been near-flawless since the fall, posting three successive clean sheets while netting three or more goals in four of their last five encounters.

The US have only lost three Nations League knockout matches, boasting a 100% home record in quarter-final outings.

Tuesday will mark their fifth international at TQL Stadium, with the Yanks undefeated at the venue, including two wins.

They are unbeaten in their last 11 internationals against Haiti, winning those last four meetings by a combined margin of 10-1.

David Badia’s men have lost their last two matches by a combined margin of 8-0 after winning their first three Nations League group outings.

The Haitians have not won a quarter-final contest in a CONCACAF competition since the 2019 Gold Cup when they were down 2-0 and stunned Canada 3-2.

They have not lost a League A encounter in this tournament when netting the opening goal since the 2023 group stage when Jamaica beat them 3-2.

Les Grenadiers can claim their first victory over the US on American soil Tuesday since 1969, when they beat them 1-0 in a World Cup qualifier in San Diego.

At 18, Julian Hall was the youngest player in the US starting 11 on Saturday, while Santiago Casteneda and Reed Baker-Whiting are seeking their first senior caps.

Christian Pulisic and Weston McKennie both featured for the first time since the World Cup this past weekend, with the former netting a brace and the latter adding one, with Hall, Auston Trusty and Folarin Balogun also scoring.

There are two Haitian players without a cap to their name, including goalkeeper Jonah Mednard and midfielder Miguel Joseph.

Fabrice Picault will hope to draw into the starting 11, as he, Ruben Providence and Yassin Fortune were among those who began on the bench for them on Saturday.

Freese; Freeman, McKenzie, Trusty, A. Robinson; McGlynn, Adams; Sullivan, Ellis, Albert; Balogun

A. Pierre; Arcus, K. Pierre, Delcroix, Experience; L. Pierre, Jean Jacques; Picault, Casimir, Isidor Fortune

The Americans have been miles ahead of their CONCACAF opponents since the World Cup concluded, and even if the squad is heavily rotated, we trust they will emerge with another comfortable victory and send Pochettino off in style

#2015. “Superb” international performance throws Scott Parker a curve ball | West Ham News

The international break has been full of surprises for West Ham‘s participants. Not all of them good. The humbling of Dinos Mavropanos Greece side by the seven goal Dutch. Tomas Soucek’s return to the Czech side marked by a late mistake. Manor Solomon’s complete exclusion from the Israel side.

Few, surely, would have expected the headlines this morning to be fêting one West Ham player who has been roundly condemned for his domestic form.

#2014. ‘Looking back…’ – Alexander Isak speaks out over penalty controversy in defeat to Arsenal

Alexander Isak has spoken out about the controversial penalty incident in which he was involved during Liverpool’s defeat to Arsenal a fortnight ago.

Five minutes after Kai Havertz netted the only goal of the match, the Reds’ number 9 had his shirt pulled by Jurrien Timber inside the box, but neither on-field referee Andy Madley nor Stuart Attwell on VAR deemed it to have been a foul.

The transgression was unmistakably clear on replays, and the Premier League’s Key Match Incidents panel has since acknowledged that a spot kick should’ve been awarded.

Speaking to reporters whilst on international duty with Sweden, Isak was asked if he felt that he should’ve had a penalty.

He replied (Aftonbladet, via Liverpool Echo): “Yeah, looking back I suppose it does look that way, but when you’re in the moment, you don’t always perceive exactly what’s happening.

“I could feel myself being pulled a bit, but not to the extent that it appears later on. I was focused on scoring. It’s hard to try to score and then fall down at the same time. I was so locked in on the goal that I didn’t really register it.”

On whether he should’ve gone to ground to try and sway the referee, Isak said: “I don’t think there’s any need to embellish or go down on purpose. Sure, if I’d had a better read on the situation, I might have made sure the referee noticed it, that’s about all you can do, but I don’t believe you need to dive or exaggerate in situations like this.

“Perhaps it shouldn’t even matter that much, given that we have VAR and systems in place to make the decisive calls in these kinds of moments.”

Isak is absolutely right in saying that a penalty should’ve been awarded, and that he shouldn’t have to act unnaturally to convince the referee to give the decision in his team’s favour.

Andoni Iraola remarked after the game that a spot kick probably would’ve been given if the Liverpool striker had gone to ground, but the onus isn’t on players to sway the officials – it’s on the latter to get these big calls right, especially with recourse to VAR.

It feels as though the debate about officiating in the Premier League will continue indefinitely, with no discernible sign of an improvement in standards from Pro Ref figurehead Howard Webb.

It’s to Isak’s great credit that he’s given such a calm and measured verdict on the penalty incident when he and his team were so blatantly wronged. He’d have had every right to complain profusely about what happened; we’d suspect that many other players would’ve done so if they were in that situation.

He certainly hasn’t let it bother him in terms of his contributions on the pitch, with the 27-year-old scoring in Liverpool’s subsequent games against Fenerbahce and Crystal Palace to take his tally for the season to eight goals in 14 matches across all competitions.

That is, in fact, the best response to the injustice which was done against him Anfield two weeks ago.

#2013. CorSport: RedBird could consider stock market listing of Milan’s new holding company

AC Milan’s new holding company, Milan Sports & Entertainment, could be publicly listed within five years according to a report.

Yesterday, RedBird announced the creation of a new holding company for the AC Milan project, named Milan Sports & Entertainment (MSE). The main goal is to have everything under one roof, from the football team to the new stadium and the NBA Europe project.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

As Cardinale himself said, there will be several new revenue streams that ultimately will benefit the football club, making it possible to invest more money in players and additional infrastructure. In short, it’s a big project and it could get even bigger.

According to Corriere dello Sport this morning, as cited by MilanNews, the launch of MSE proves that RedBird and Cardinale have a long-term plan for the club. A listing on the stock market cannot be ruled out within the next five years either, opening the company up to further investment.

Only two football clubs in Italy are publicly traded, namely Juventus and Lazio, meaning fans can effectively become shareholders. However, it should be noted that these shares rarely come with any real power, used more as a way of raising funds than anything else.

Outside of Italy, clubs like Borussia Dortmund and Manchester United are also publicly listed, so it’s not like Milan would be moving into uncharted territory.

By Saikat Mandal | 15 Nov 2026 19:32

Manchester United are reportedly showing interest in Fulham defender Calvin Bassey ahead of the January transfer window.

The Red Devils are languishing in 18th place in the Premier League table, and Mauricio Pochettino has a huge task on his hands to pull the club out of their current predicament.

While his primary objective will be to steer United away from the relegation zone, the club must quickly turn their attention to the winter transfer window, with strengthening the defence an urgent priority.

The 26-year-old has featured nine times in the Premier League this season, and his experience could prove valuable to Man Utd, who have already conceded 19 goals in 10 matches.

Bassey offers considerable physical presence and pace at the back, two qualities that the Red Devils have arguably lacked this season.

It would be difficult for Bassey to dismiss an offer from Man Utd outright, regardless of their current position in the league.

The defender's contract at Craven Cottage runs until next summer, although Fulham have the option to extend it by a further 12 months.

Arvada Arbeloa regards Bassey as one of the best defenders in the Premier League, but whether Fulham can hold on to him if the Red Devils table a tempting offer remains a major question.

#2011. Andy Burnham and his comments on the 3pm Saturday blackout got me thinking

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

The headline declared that Andy Burnham has urged caution on scrapping the 3pm Saturday TV blackout.

Ahead of this latest international break I was at the Fulham v Newcastle United game, the novelty of it being a rare 3pm kick-off for NUFC.

The BBC article that I was reading, stated: “The blackout originated in the 1960s when Burnley chairman Bob Lord encouraged the EFL to oppose television coverage of 3pm Saturday matches.”

I understand the sentiments expressed by Andy Burnham, as he doesn’t want to be seen as upsetting the lower league clubs who are dependent on match day receipts and the peripheral spending.

However, when you look at the amount of games in the Premier League played outside the Saturday 3pm kick-off, you begin to wonder.

The working man’s game where you could rock up to St James’ Park with a belly full of ale for a 3pm kick-off and pay at the turnstiles are a thing of the past and long gone.

Take a look at the Newcastle United fixtures so far this season and you will see Fulham really was novelty.

In these first five months of the 2026-27 Premier League season only three 3pm Saturday kick-offs for Newcastle United, home to Hull and away to Fulham, plus Ipswich away next month.

All of these Premier League games played outside of the 3pm Saturday slot is a boon for lower league clubs. Due to technology, I can watch Newcastle play at 3pm on a Saturday even when I don’t get a ticket for the match.

But the 3pm Saturday kick-off is such a rarity it has become an irrelevance.

As the Newcastle United games are now shown at an increasingly ridiculous range of times, that frees up Saturday afternoon for me and my mates to go down to Dulwich Hamlet on a Saturday afternoon and have a pint of Peckham pale ale on the terracing while watching live football in the Isthmian Premier League.

So as me and my lad fail to get home tickets for Newcastle United on a regular basis now (no need for tiny violins), we are down the Hamlet on a Saturday afternoon with hundreds of other like minded Premier League team supporting people, who simply want to see live football kicking off at a proper time.

One transfer insider has claimed that Liverpool may be ‘quite optimistic’ over agreeing a new contract for a high-profile first-team player.

Since turning 18 in August, Rio Ngumoha has been eligible for a longer-term deal at Anfield and, with it, a significant wage increase; and Fabrizio Romano indicated in October that ‘active conversations’ are ongoing over a prospective extension for the teenage winger.

Lewis Steele hinted that a new deal for the youngster should be a matter of when and not if, and the player himself said in an interview last week that it was a ‘no-brainer’ to swap Chelsea’s academy for the Reds two years ago.

Speaking on the Transfer Insider podcast for Football Insider, Pete O’Rourke also talked up the probability of Ngumoha signing a new contract at Liverpool, with both parties likely to want that conclusion.

The journalist said: “Ngumoha is happy at Liverpool. Liverpool are very happy with him. He came out in an interview earlier this week saying that his move to Liverpool was a no-brainer, that he was happy that he made that decision to leave Chelsea for Liverpool.

“I would imagine there’s a willingness from all parties to get a new contract done, so I’d imagine Liverpool are quite optimistic that they will get this sorted.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

With Ngumoha having been given his big break into senior football at Liverpool and featuring regularly under Andoni Iraola this season, we’re also confident that he’ll pen a new contract at Anfield in the coming months.

He’s currently on £35,000 per week from the deal that he agreed in September 2025, which puts him among the Reds’ lower first-team earners (Capology), but we’d suspect that’d increase to six figures with the next extension that he signs in L4.

Since breaking into the senior setup just over a year ago, the winger has never looked back, taking to the elite level with a swagger and a confidence which is rare for players as young as him and even winning a handful of England caps.

Liverpool have other major contract situations to resolve over the next few months – Alisson Becker and Virgil van Dijk are nearing the end of their deals, and speculation continues to abound over Alexis Mac Allister – but keeping Ngumoha at the club for the long-term would be, to use his phrasing, a no-brainer.

It might take another little while yet for full confirmation to arrive, but we share O’Rourke’s optimism that the teenage forward will pen a new long-term contract at Anfield in the near future.

#2008. Incredible story as Newcastle United teenager creates history with Brazil

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Newcastle United teenager Matheos Ferreira has made history in the colours of Brazil.

The exciting 18-year-old winger got his first ever call up for his country this month.

Matheos Ferreira named in the Brazil Under 20s squad for a double header with Peru.

He was an unused sub on Friday when the young Brazil stars won 2-0.

Then on Monday he made history, Matheos Ferreira becoming the first player developed at the Newcastle United Academy to go on to represent Brazil at international level.

The 18-year-old is from Berwick but is eligible to represent the country through his Brazilian father, Thiago.

Not only did Matheos Ferreira make his first ever start for the Brazil Under 20s on Monday, it only took him 14 minutes to score!

The United winger putting Brazil into the lead against Peru Under 20s in Belem.

— Bradley Robson (@bradrobson2605) November 17, 2026

Matheos Ferreira seeing his dream international debut get even better when he also supplied an assist as the Brazil youngsters routed the opposition and won 9-0 against Peru.

The Newcastle United Academy star talked to official NUFC club media from Brazil ahead of his debut: “I had to start training as soon as I got there but I think it’s shown how far I have come as a player because I wasn’t too nervous or anxious… I am doing the thing I love the most, playing football, and it was nice to get on the pitch and train with the squad. It’s been busy! The culture is completely different here but I really like it. We’re having to train in the evening as it is usually over 30 degrees during the day. Since the first training session, I’ve felt very welcome by the lads and the coaches as well.”

Matheos Ferreira also qualifies to play potentially for England and Italy (his mam’s Italian).

The winger joined the Newcastle United Academy in 2020 after playing for Berwick Juniors and Cramlington Juniors and recalled the moment he found out he’d got his first Brazil call up: “My first reaction was just pure joy. I was so happy. My parents wanted to tell me first before I checked my phone but it was still a great moment to share with them, who were both very emotional. I think it’s a reward for how I’ve been playing but also how I’ve managed to conduct myself off the pitch with my recovery, willingness to learn and reflecting on how I can improve on the matches I’ve played in. It’s an amazing achievement but I don’t want this to be the last. I will keep pushing on and try to get that next call-up or progress into the first-team. Once I reach one level, it’s about getting to the next one. It doesn’t stop there. We’ve got the South American (Youth Football) Championship in January and the Under-20 World Cup is next year so I’m pushing really hard to try and get into both squads. I’m doing everything I can to try and make my international debut. It would mean a lot. I haven’t got this big pressure of needing to do well – I just want to get on that pitch, show what I can do and do what I love the most.”

Matheos Ferreira remembering: “My first memory of Brazilian football would be my dad showing videos of Ronaldinho, R9 and Neymar,” he added. “The first game I watched live was at Wembley between England and Brazil and Neymar played. I think it finished goalless though! The interest they showed me and the project they have was a big reason [to accept the call-up]. Brazil is a big country so to be recognised by them is amazing. It’s a big opportunity and an honour to represent them.”

The 18-year-old rising Newcastle United star is buzzing with how the 2026-27 season has kicked off, for club and country: “I’ve really enjoyed the start to this season. The coaches trust me as I’ve been playing in different positions for the Under-21s; wing-back, as a winger or a number ten. I think they know what I can provide for the team. I think its shows the qualities I have. Playing as a right wing-back shows I can defend, put my body on the line and then it’s about showing my strengths going forward. I’ve embraced the challenges of switching positions, thinking about the tactical side of the game.”

A brilliant moment on Monday for Matheos Ferreira and here’s to many more appearances (and goals!) in the colours of Brazil AND Newcastle United.

By Saikat Mandal | 15 Nov 2026 20:01

Arsenal are reportedly interested in signing Will Lankshear during the January transfer window, but Middlesbrough have no intention of letting their prized striker leave.

The Gunners have been linked with a move for the 21-year-old, who has been in sensational goalscoring form for Boro this season.

Lankshear joined the Riverside outfit from Tottenham Hotspur for £20m during the summer transfer window and wasted little time establishing himself as one of their key players.

The young striker has scored 15 goals in 16 appearances for Boro, helping the Teessiders climb to second in the Championship table, level on points with Birmingham City and Stoke City.

According to The Sun, Boro are determined to resist any bids for Lankshear and have slapped a £70m price tag on the striker.

If Boro secure promotion to the Premier League next season, they could stand to make more than double the fee they paid for him, meaning a January sale would make little financial sense.

Leeds United and Newcastle United have also reportedly watched him in action this season, while Spurs are keeping a close eye on his development.

Tottenham do not have a buy-back clause in Lankshear's contract, as such clauses are not permitted in transfers between Premier League and EFL clubs.

However, the North London club do have matching rights, meaning they can match any offer another club has agreed with Middlesbrough for the striker in the future.

Mikel Arteta could be looking to bring in a new striker in January after Arsenal failed to land their top target, Julian Alvarez, during the summer window.

Viktor Gyokeres has managed just one Premier League start this season and has cut a somewhat subdued figure, struggling to make a significant impact so far.

The Gunners are also looking to strengthen their wide attacking options, with RB Leipzig's Antonio Nusa heavily linked with a move to the Emirates Stadium.

While Lankshear is enjoying a fabulous campaign, it would make sense for Arsenal to assess his progress over a full season rather than spend a sizeable sum to secure his services in January.

In Episode 17 of The Mag Pod, we find Jamie, Simon, and Hutch discussing relegation, again! You can play episode 17 on the audio player above or use your favourite podcast platforms including Spotify, Apple Podcasts, Amazon Music, YouTube, and Acast.

Listen to the latest episode of The Mag Pod! Join Jamie, Simon, and Hutch for unfiltered football debate.

Jamie Smith, Simon Cahill and David Hutchinson revisit Newcastle United’s 2015-16 relegation season under the ownership of Mike Ashley, examining the failures under Steve McClaren, the arrival of Rafa Benítez and whether there are lessons to be learned amid the concerns surrounding the current 2026-27 campaign.

There’s a look back at the performances of Georginio Wijnaldum, Aleksandar Mitrović, Fabricio Coloccini and Moussa Sissoko, as well as some personal memories of the campaign, including a frustrating afternoon at Old Trafford and a particularly miserable pre-Christmas encounter with Aston Villa.

#2003. Gustavo Nunes, Kevin, Vitor Reis and Rodrigo Muniz fight for playing time in the Premier League

By Alexis Pereira | 15 Nov 2026 20:06

Four Brazilians are fighting for game time at the start of the 2026-27 Premier League season: Gustavo Nunes at Brentford, Kevin and Rodrigo Muniz at Fulham, and Vitor Reis at Manchester City. They are young players seeking to establish themselves and a centre-forward trying to regain his prominence in England.

The Brazilian presence in the Premier League is not limited to the players who regularly appear among the standout names. Alongside those who have won a place and become protagonists in England, there are also those trying to turn occasional chances into a longer run of games. None of the four has yet established himself among his manager’s main options, although for different reasons and in different circumstances. Some have barely featured in league games, while others have been used during matches but without enough time to build a run.

Gustavo Nunes joined Brentford in August 2024 after catching the eye at Gremio. Developed in the Brazilian club’s youth system, the forward made his professional debut in February that year and quickly earned a place. He played 40 games for the first team, scoring seven goals and providing four assists, numbers that helped attract English interest.

The move did not have the expected start. Physical problems delayed his debut for Brentford, who were only able to use him for the first time in April 2025. That season, he made three Premier League appearances, always from the bench, and had few opportunities to show his qualities.

The search for more minutes led the club to loan him to Swansea City in January 2026. In the Championship, he played 12 games and provided one assist. After returning to Brentford, he rejoined the squad but has still not played in a Premier League game in 2026-27, alternating between being left out of the squad and being an unused substitute. At 20, he is trying to find a place in an attack where he still has to win the trust of boss Keith Andrews.

Kevin, a Fulham forward, is another Brazilian looking for a bigger role. Developed at Palmeiras, he played for Shakhtar Donetsk before moving to the Premier League. In Ukraine, he stood out for his dribbling and attacking involvement, with 17 goals and 10 assists in 57 games between 2024 and 2025.

Fulham signed him in September 2025. In his first season in England, Kevin had opportunities throughout the campaign but did not establish himself as a starter. He made 26 Premier League appearances, nine of them as a starter, with one goal and two assists. In the early weeks of 2026-27, however, his involvement has shrunk. He has played five times in the league, always as a substitute, for only 75 minutes. In the EFL Cup, he was used in all three games for the Cottagers, two as a starter. Without a goal or assist so far, the 23-year-old is trying to use the minutes he gets to show he can be a more frequent alternative in Fulham’s attack.

Rodrigo Muniz has the most established record in the Premier League of the four. Signed by Fulham in August 2021 after a spell at Flamengo, the centre-forward needed time to adapt to English football. Before winning a place in the London side, he was loaned to Middlesbrough, for whom he played 17 games and scored two goals in the Championship.

His first big moment at Fulham came in 2023-24, when he scored nine goals in 26 Premier League games, 18 of them as a starter, and ten goals in 33 matches in all competitions. The following year he kept an important role, with eight goals in 31 top-flight games, only eight as a starter, and 11 goals in 36 matches across all competitions. In 2025-26, however, his numbers dropped sharply due to muscle injuries: 25 appearances and only one goal.

The trend of reduced use continues this season. Muniz has played in eight Premier League games, all from the bench, for 96 minutes. Despite the limited space, he scored against Newcastle United on 7 November, his first goal of the current Premier League campaign and the third of the year, as he has also scored twice in the EFL Cup. At 25, the centre-forward is trying to use that kind of opportunity to regain ground in the battle to lead the attack.

Vitor Reis’ situation is slightly different. Signed by Manchester City in January 2025 after impressing at Palmeiras, the centre-back arrived in England with the status of one of the leading prospects in Brazilian defending. The investment by the English club reinforced expectations around his development, but competition for a place in the defensive system has always been an obstacle.

In the first half of 2025, he had very limited involvement before being loaned to Girona for the following season. In Spain, he found the space needed to gain experience in one of Europe’s top leagues. He played 36 La Liga games, with more than 3,000 minutes on the pitch, and scored one goal and provided one assist.

His return to Manchester City, however, did not bring an immediate change in outlook. In this Premier League season, Reis has made just one appearance, playing one minute off the bench. He has been given opportunities in other competitions, such as the EFL Cup (two full starts and one goal) and the Champions League (18 minutes against AEK Athens), but is still far from a run of games in the league. At 20, the centre-back is still adapting to the demands of English football and trying to turn the experience gained in Spain into a place in boss Enzo Maresca’s squad.

#2002. Jacob Murphy is not our future but he IS the here and now

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

In the grand and often unforgiving theatre of Premier League football, where stars are minted in bursts of brilliance and extinguished by the next transfer window, there are players whose value is measured not solely in highlight reels but in the quiet accumulation of purpose.

Jacob Murphy belongs to that rarer company.

At 31, the Newcastle United winger continues to embody a particular kind of professional resilience—one forged in loans, tempered by reinvention, and now expressed in moments that still make the away end rise as one.

I know, we’ve heard the complaints of many fans and pundits that Jacob Murphy is “not good enough”, that he disappears for long stretches during the match, that we need an upgrade at the position. Maybe. The lad is not perfect or to everyone’s liking but he is my cup of tea. He produces with first-time crosses into the box, always gives 100%, readily gets back on defence, and adds a bit of needed comic relief.

Born in Wembley on 24 February 1995 to parents with roots in NE England, Murphy carried Newcastle in his blood long before he wore the shirt. A boyhood Magpie who grew up visiting family in Gateshead, he and his twin brother Josh cut their teeth at Norwich City’s academy. Together they helped win the FA Youth Cup in 2013. Jacob’s path thereafter was the classic English apprenticeship of the lower leagues: temporary homes at Swindon, Southend, Blackpool, Scunthorpe, Colchester, and, most formatively, a season-long stay at Coventry City in 2015-16 where he scored ten goals and announced himself as a player of genuine threat. Returning to Norwich, he produced a breakthrough campaign of nearly double figures in goals and assists, enough to persuade Rafa Benítez to bring him to St James’ Park in the summer of 2017 for a fee in the region of £12 million.

The early years on Tyneside were not seamless. There were loans—to West Bromwich Albion and Sheffield Wednesday—and the familiar struggle of a young wide player trying to impose himself in a club that was itself searching for direction (certainly, Steve Bruce was not the man to coach him up).

What changed everything was the arrival of Eddie Howe.

Under Howe, Jacob Murphy was transformed from squad option into indispensable operator. He became the energetic wide presence who pressed, crossed, tracked, and, with increasing frequency, delivered. The 2024-25 season marked his high-water mark: eight Premier League goals and a dozen assists, a body of work that placed him among the league’s most productive creators from the flank. He scored in the Carabao Cup semi-final against Arsenal and provided a decisive assist in the final as Newcastle United ended a 70-year wait for a major domestic trophy. For a player once dismissed by some as a useful squad man, it was validation of the highest order.

Murphy’s assets have never been those of the purest technician or the most glamorous dribbler. He is direct. He is tireless. He possesses a left foot capable of bending a ball from distance with sudden, almost unfair venom, and a right foot that can pick out a player in the box. Was Alexander Isak worth the money Liverpool paid without the assists of Murphy? I’d argue that we got top money from the Reds for the rat – and Murphy’s crosses were a major contributor. His willingness to occupy the spaces that make others look better. He crosses with purpose, contributes defensively without complaint, and brings a structural intelligence that managers prize.

In a squad that has undergone significant change—younger faces arriving, senior voices departing—his experience has become a form of quiet leadership. Even after being omitted from the formal player leadership group under new head coach Matthias Jaissle, Murphy has spoken of an unchanged responsibility: to add value, to set standards, to help the younger players understand what the Premier League demands week after week.

This season has been more measured than the explosion of 2024-25. Minutes have been shared; the goal tally has been slower to climb. Yet the importance remains as he’s more dependable than Anthony Elanga and much more experienced that Matias Fernandez-Pardo.

On a November afternoon at Craven Cottage, with Newcastle searching for a response after consecutive defeats, Murphy produced the kind of moment that defines him. Intercepting a loose pass, he drove forward, cut inside, and from fully 25 yards unleashed a curling left-footed strike that left Bernd Leno helpless. The goal was his first of the campaign. It was also a reminder.

Three minutes later Fulham equalised (of course they did) but the point was earned in part because of that individual quality and the industry that preceded it. Days earlier he had provided an assist in a clean-sheet victory at Crystal Palace. The pattern is familiar: when Newcastle need a spark or a measure of control on the flank, Murphy is often the player trusted to provide it.

There is something almost old-fashioned in his story. In an era of astronomical fees and instantaneous celebrity, Murphy has built a career through persistence, adaptation, and an unshowy professionalism. He has scored against Manchester City in his early days, netted a brace against Tottenham (including a scorcher!), contributed to European nights and a first major trophy in generations. He has survived the doubts that accompany any player who does not fit the neatest marketing narrative. Now, with his contract situation under discussion and interest from elsewhere already rejected by the club, he continues to state the obvious with clarity: he knows what he brings.

I am not advocating that Jacob Murphy is our future but he IS the here and now. The best we have at his position and, until we can get in a player with better talent and upside, indispensable for the team this season.

For Newcastle United in this transitional season under Jaissle, that contribution—energy, experience, the capacity for the sudden decisive strike—remains quietly essential. Jacob Murphy does not demand the spotlight. He simply continues to occupy the spaces where the game is still won, one determined run, one precise cross, one unforgettable curler at a time.

In the long narrative of a club that has known both glory and patience, his is a chapter written in steady ink. I think its time to give him some respect. 🎙️ THE MAG PODCAST Ep 15: Fulham frustration, Newcastle United’s season report card and Relegation fears Listen to the latest episode of The Mag Pod! #2001. Championship data highlights exactly what West Ham’s midfield is still missing

A fascinating piece of Championship analysis from Loft Insights on X may provide an uncomfortable reminder of where West Ham’s midfield falls short.

The graphic plots central midfielders based on two key metrics: line-breaking passes per 90 minutes and ball-winning actions per 90 minutes. Put simply, it measures which players are able to progress the ball through opposition lines while also contributing defensively.

The most interesting takeaway for me was not necessarily which players stand out, but where West Ham’s own midfield profiles sit on the chart.

The Championship’s elite midfielders increasingly occupy the top-right quadrant, combining progression and defensive intensity. That is why the chart identifies Norwich City’s Kenny McLean as one of the Championship’s most complete midfielders, posting outstanding line-breaking numbers while maintaining strong defensive output, despite only featuring for ten games out of fifteen due to an ankle injury.

Meanwhile, Portsmouth’s Ebou Adams is highlighted as a “defensive monster”, producing exceptional ball-winning statistics while still offering significant progression. Sheffield United’s Kalvin Phillips (yes the same player that flopped on loan at West Ham!), Queens Park Rangers’ Jonathan Varane and Norwich’s Jacob Wright also occupy impressive positions, demonstrating the ability to impact both sides of the game.

Mohamadou Kanté is viewed as a dynamic ball-carrying midfielder with strong physical attributes, but his game is built more around energy and transition play than elite progression metrics. Arne Engels offers technical quality and creativity, yet is generally more comfortable operating higher up the pitch than acting as a defensive controller.

The data is only based on players who have played an average of 540 mins so one omission is Tomas Souček, whose strengths have always been obvious. The Czech international on paper would arguably be the Championships most effective midfield goalscorer (3 in 7 appearances so far) and I’d expect him to feature highly for aerial presence. However, if plotted on a graph measuring line-breaking passes and ball-winning volume, he would likely owe more to his physicality and attacking threat than his ability to dictate possession through midfield.

That perhaps explains why West Ham can sometimes appear disconnected between defence and attack.

Too often there is a reliance on direct balls into attacking areas rather than building through the centre of the pitch. Equally, when possession is lost, the midfield does not always possess the combination of mobility and defensive output needed to regain control quickly.

West Ham arguably have midfielders who can create and win duels. What they appear to lack is a genuine “two-way” midfielder capable of consistently ranking highly in both categories.

That was precisely what Declan Rice offered during his time at the club. His ability to recover possession and immediately progress the ball remains incredibly difficult to replace.

The reality is Rice was never truly replaced, although finding a like-for-like successor was always going to be a near-impossible task

Former West Ham midfielder James Ward-Prowse’s position on the chart is also interesting. A casualty of Nuno’s reign, he ranks among the highest players for line-breaking passes but has one of the lowest ball-winning outputs. Ward-Prowse excels at progressing possession but offers relatively little defensive contribution compared to the league’s most complete midfielders.

Above all the data serves as a reminder that Koppen’s recruitment and Parker’s existing choices for midfield should focus less on individual statistics and more on complete profiles.

Because the numbers suggest that is where Championship matches are increasingly won.

I have been a season ticket holder since the late eighties, so experienced the highs and lows of being a West Ham supporter. I previously wrote for OLAS and have contributed to a number of football publications in the past.

I think there is nothing wrong with the Midfield. There is just a problem with the short pass mentality. The day of playing short passes across midfield are over in English football. You need decent long passes with good trapping and decent positive movement. How many of West Ham’s passes are square ball or back passes ? Far to many. Particularly back passes are all to often caught on to giving away needless goals. Walker-Peters is a really good example. Having moved forward beating someone, he then passes back in midfield, or worst still carries the ball backwards towards midfield or defence. Play positively, avoid back passes, learn to pass well and trap well and you have a very good midfield. Orford, Kante and other young players are far better at doing this, than the older players.

#2000. Fabrizio Romano warns of ‘increasingly complicated’ situation which is brewing at Liverpool

Fabrizio Romano has warned that the future of one player at Liverpool is ‘becoming increasingly complicated’.

Long-serving goalkeeper Alisson Becker is into the final year of his contract at Anfield, but he recently expressed his desire to extend his stay at the club, and his agent has reportedly entered ‘preliminary talks’ with LFC chiefs over a prospective new deal.

With the Brazilian’s status as number 1 firmly intact, it leaves Giorgi Mamardashvili playing a backup role and having to be patient for opportunities, a situation that he might feel a compulsion to change in the foreseeable future.

In a video on his eponymous YouTube channel, Romano outlined that the Georgian mightn’t be prepared to wait for his chance for much longer if Alisson were to extend his contract.

The transfer reporter said: “Liverpool are no longer masters of Alisson’s destiny, let’s put it that way. Last summer they were able to say, ‘Stay with us, we’ll extend for another year, we’ll activate the option.’ Now that option has expired, so Alisson can decide his future.

“There is certainly a possibility that Alisson will remain at Liverpool. However, the situation involving him and Giorgi Mamardashvili is becoming increasingly complicated.

“This is because Mamardashvili is not a player who wants to remain a backup goalkeeper indefinitely. He is playing second fiddle while waiting for the door to open for a starting spot at Liverpool and at some point, a decision will have to be made.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Romano’s information echoes that of James Pearce a few weeks ago when the latter indicated that, if Alisson were to stay put, his understudy wouldn’t accept a third season of playing backup to the Brazil veteran.

The role of a second-choice goalkeeper is a peculiar one. They’re only one twist of fate away from getting what could be their big break, but they could be left waiting months (if not years) for that sliding doors moment.

Mamardashvili hasn’t yet managed to seriously challenge our number 1 for a place in the starting XI, but the Georgian has produced some strong performances in the Carabao Cup this season, including one world-class save against Tottenham in the third round in September.

Even his status as Alisson’s immediate deputy could come under threat from next year once Lucca Brughmans arrives from Genk, although that chain of command would be contingent on the Brazilian’s future at Liverpool.

We can see it from Mamardashvili’s perspective – he’s 26 now and won’t want to fritter away too much of his career warming the bench – but it’s essential for the Reds to have a solid succession plan in place for life after their long-serving number 1, whose world-class presence will be extremely difficult to replace.

#1999. 9 rule changes to help the referee cut out cheating and make the game fairer

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

The referee and his role in what’s wrong with football.

One of the many problems with football in England is the refereeing.

Not necessarily the refs themselves, more the ever-changing guidance and policies they are expected to obey when it comes to their refereeing.

The Premier League is the world’s most popular, watched all around the globe on television in far higher numbers than any other rival.

It is a money-spinning product that cannot afford to lose its pre-eminent position. Those in charge, such as Richard Masters, the Premier League’s chief executive, have millions of reasons to protect the brand.

In his particular case, 2.6 million for the financial year ending on July 31, 2025. That included a £1.1m bonus awarded in part for his help in negotiating record-breaking broadcasting deals with Sky, TNT and Amazon.

That £2.6m remuneration package (as they like to say in the City of London) was £700,000 up on the previous year. Don’t expect any reduction when the 2025-26 figures are lodged at Companies House . . .

The Premier League’s popularity relies on more than having some of the world’s best players. It also depends on the characteristic style of play being distinctly different from La Liga or the Bundesliga or Serie A. Which is where the refereeing comes in.

You might believe a referee’s primary role is to ensure, to the best of his ability, the game is played fairly. You might be right, though I suspect the job of protecting the brand has become the driving force for the man in the middle and his colleagues.

The more free kicks, the less attractive the spectacle. Those in charge of the Premier League cannot afford a stop-start product, because viewer figures are paramount.

Pro Ref knows this, the players know this, the managers know this. That’s why so many fouls go unpunished. Not because the referees should go to Specsavers. They see them and choose to ignore them.

It’s the coward’s way. Or should that be Howard’s Way? Mr Webb, the head of Pro Ref, was pilloried when VAR kept halting the action. He responded by telling the boys and girls at Stockley Park to intervene in only the most extreme cases.

Outcome: a non-decision by the ref is not corrected by the VAR.

The most blatant mistakes are later scrutinised by the Premier League’s key match incidents panel. Its verdicts read like an Orwellian nightmare.

In a typical case, a penalty is not awarded for foul play. The VAR, obeying Howard’s Way, looks and agrees. Days later, the key match incidents panel says: “A penalty was probably the right call but VAR was correct in doing nothing. If the ref had blown for the foul, the VAR would have agreed.”

So there you have it. Whichever call the referee makes is correct. It must be, because the VAR backed him up. Reminds me of the olden days when the referee’s decision was final.

Before each season starts, changes are announced to the way the laws of the game will be enforced. Among recent initiatives was the five-second countdown on throws and goal kicks if the referee detected time wasting. They are rarely enforced because the threat of being penalised has encouraged quicker play, as intended. There’s also a 10-second limit for a substituted player to leave the field.

Nobody would argue against those changes, though they smack of window dressing when much more important problems are being ignored. Here are just a few suggestions to make the game fairer.

1. Warn any player who refuses to retreat 10 yards promptly from an opponent’s free kick. The second time he or a teammate does it, book the offender. Third time, red card.

2. Issue a yellow card for pushing whenever no attempt is made to play the ball.

3. Award a throw-in to the other team if the ball is not released from behind the head. Or if both feet are not grounded behind the touchline. Or if the throw is taken more than two yards forward of the right point. Players know.

4) Book any player who pulls an opponent’s shirt, shorts or socks.

5) Stop players taking free kicks from the wrong spot. If they do it again, book them. Keepers in particular move the ball up the field or towards their goal with impunity, knowing the referee will do nothing.

6) A yellow card for all offences of dissent, either physical or verbal, directed at the referee or his assistants. Including the captain.

7) An automatic card to any player who dives. In the opponents’ penalty area, make it a red.

8) Add on at least one minute for every goal celebration.

9) Play an advantage if there is the chance of one but go back and book any player who has fouled off the ball.

You might think there would be a blizzard of yellow and red cards. I believe the far more likely consequence would be a massive reduction in gamesmanship, cheating, time wasting and other examples of the dark arts that are blighting the beautiful game.

Once players realised they couldn’t foul with impunity, they would quickly learn to play the game as a sport, rather than as a cynical win-at-all-costs exercise.

#1997. “Make them excel and get better”- Returning hero’s stated West Ham ambition

Along with regime change and boardroom change this year, there has been evolution in the West Ham United coaching department as Nuno’s team departed along with  their Portuguese boss and Scott Parker brought in his own hand-picked replacements.

As we covered last week, alongside the headline hires, one of the lesser known appointments was for former West Ham hero – and son of hero – David Martin to rejoin West Ham’s coaching team as the Academy’s head of goal keeping.

David Martin’s West Ham career was short but never-to-be-forgotten

Martin has been quick to praise the talent available to him in his new role: Speaking to West Ham’s web site, the 40 year old confirmed his own methodical approach:

“I enjoy having a plan, making the very most of myself and my abilities, being a good person and making people around me better…

“That’s what the role is – creating a competitive environment where people can learn and improve under pressure. I’ve got two very good young goalkeepers in the development squad – Fin Hooper and Lanre Awesu – and it’s an unbelievable competition between them and I want that to make them excel and get better.”

Of course with former academy graduate Finlay Herrick now officially Scott Parker’s third choice keeper, (and not forgetting Mason Terry who is out on loan) the Hammers do have an embarrassment of riches in their ‘up and coming’ goal keeping department.

It can only be a matter of time before Herrick progresses – something tells me this might be sooner than we think – and it is good to see that West Ham are embracing their heritage with an appointment like Martin’s to a pivotal post within the club.

#1996. PSG, Liverpool, Bayern Munich and Chelsea eyeing Man City Josko Gvardiol

By Alexis Pereira | 15 Nov 2026 20:23

Paris Saint-Germain are reportedly prepared to compete with Barcelona for a Premier League defender the Catalan club dream of lining up in central defence alongside Pau Cubarsi. According to El Nacional, that defender is Manchester City’s Josko Gvardiol.

It is no secret that Barcelona want to use the January transfer window to sign a new centre-back. Germany international Jonathan Tah, whom Bayern Munich have no intention of losing, is no longer an option, but the Catalan hierarchy have activated other profiles. Hansi Flick’s side have also positioned themselves for Gvardiol.

Able to play in central defence, the Croatia international is most often used as a left-back by boss Enzo Maresca. Across the Premier League and the Champions League, the 24-year-old has started nine times in that position since the beginning of 2026-27. But it is for central defence that Barcelona are thinking strongly about his arrival, with an improbable chance of success as early as January 2027.

According to El Nacional, the plan is to make him a future ‘ideal partner’ for Cubarsi, in an area where Eric Garcia and Andreas Christensen are options with limited time left. Barcelona will have to convince Manchester City to sell a player of this calibre, who has a contract until 2031 and a reported market value of around £64m.

Another obstacle for Barcelona is fierce competition from other European powers. According to the same source, PSG, Liverpool, Bayern Munich and Chelsea are also interested in the former Dinamo Zagreb player.

Like their illustrious rivals, the French capital club are closely monitoring possible sanctions against Manchester City, who are threatened with relegation because of their financial irregularities and who, if such a sentence is confirmed, could be forced to sell all of their leading players.

PSG’s reported interest runs into two questions, however. Until proven otherwise, the double Champions League holders are not prioritising a left-back, preferring a right-sided centre-back and a right-back to back up Achraf Hakimi.

Gvardiol may also be more tempted by a challenge at Barcelona, in a squad where competition looks less fierce than at PSG, with Willian Pacho in central defence and Nuno Mendes on the left.

#1995. The Mike Ashley relegations pre Newcastle United takeover and lessons to be learnt

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

I hold my hands up that I was guilty of a bit of an oversight during The Mag Podcast last week.

“Those who do not learn from the past are doomed to repeat it” – George Santayana

I half remembered the quote above and threw it to my co-host Hutch on The Mag Pod to try and recite it verbatim, as he likes history and stuff like that.

There were two errors involved to be fair, me for putting him on the spot like that, and Hutch for being as thick as mince.

Jamie puts Hutch on the spot over Newcastle United’s relegation history

Anyway, I’ve since found the appropriate wording and replicated as a starting point here, as a way of conveying what we’ve been doing on The Mag Pod as we tried to fill the ongoing international break. Basically, there has been some chatter and paranoia that the issues this Newcastle United side are facing this season could well lead to a relegation battle. If it does turn out that way, it won’t be any of our first rodeos.

However, it’s fair to say that many of those Mike Ashley era struggles ended fairly benignly, with the drop avoided. On occasions this was comfortably, at times it was squeaky, but it didn’t really matter as long as you lived to fight another day. Unfortunately, there were exceptions.

So, to try and learn the lessons of history, we have used this round of podcasts to look at the Mike Ashley seasons where it went terribly wrong.

Late last week the first instalment (Episode 16) dropped, as we took a walk through the chaotic 2008-09 season. The follow-up, reliving the relegation of 2015-16 (Episode 17), which is out now.

These serve as both a wander through times gone by and a study in what we can learn.

Ideally, listeners may feel better about current circumstances in comparison with the poor decisions, awful form and careless business that led to highly avoidable seasons away from the Premier League under the previous regime.

Unfortunately there may be times when certain things ring true and we appear in real danger of breaking Mr Santayana’s above rule.

There is a third instalment to come as well, but alas we are a bit wet behind the lugs to fully recount the demotion of 1988-89.

Instead, a slight change of tack is incoming where Thursday’s edition (Episode 18) will see a review of the 2020-21 season, the final year before the Newcastle United takeover. This is to give a perspective on how far we have come, the impact of the considerable changes since and to hopefully make you all feel better you’re no longer looking at Steve Bruce.

Spoiler alert, but the general overall conclusion of these editions is that more time and consideration is needed in the current circumstances, to really have a full and proper idea of how badly it may compare to some of our darker times. However, there are things in there that may very well resonate.

Please enjoy The Mag Podcast and we’d love your feedback on what we have done so far and suggestions for the future in the commenting section below.
